justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon reflect a best-guess projection of the central value—707.06 in this case. This suggests an expectation that, in the absence of a major shock, current trends or underlying dynamics (such as prices, demand, or other relevant variables) will persist over time. These estimates are typically derived from statistical models, trends in historical data, or assumptions about stability in the system being forecasted. In this case, the model assumes no significant directional movements over 1 day, 1 week, or even 1 month, hence the constant point estimate across all three horizons.

The confidence intervals, or ranges of possible outcomes, capture uncertainties that grow as the forecast horizon extends. Over 1 day, there’s less time for fluctuations or external events to have a large impact, so the interval is relatively narrow (700.99 to 713.13). Over a week and especially a month, there is more time for random variations, unforeseen events, or shifts in the underlying dynamics to take effect. This is why the intervals widen noticeably, from a 38.34 range over a week to more than 100 points over a month. Factors like market volatility, external shocks (e.g., policy changes, macroeconomic developments), or noise in the data all influence how uncertain we are about outcomes further out into the future.

There are always specific risks or events that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. For example, major unexpected disruptions such as geopolitical conflicts, regulatory changes, or economic shocks could create scenarios not captured in the current forecast. Other possibilities include heightened volatility due to speculative activity, unforeseen changes in supply and demand dynamics, or errors in the underlying assumptions of the model. If such events occur, they could render the confidence intervals too narrow or the point estimates inaccurate, as the model cannot fully anticipate or incorporate these extreme scenarios ahead of time.
